:::{.callout-tip}
## R for Python users

| Python | R | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `x = 5` | `x <- 5` | `<-` is the conventional assignment in R; `=` works but is avoided at the top level |
| `import numpy as np` | `library(terra)` | Load packages with `library()`, install once with `install.packages("terra")` |
| `a[0]` | `a[1]` | R is **1-indexed** |
| `df.pivot(...)` | `pivot_wider(...)` | Reshaping is done with `tidyr` functions |
| `df.method()` chaining | `df \|> func()` | R uses the native pipe `\|>` to chain operations |
| `None` / `float('nan')` | `NA` | R uses `NA` for all missing values; most functions have an `na.rm = TRUE` argument |
| `arr.shape` | `dim(x)`, `nrow(x)`, `ncol(x)` | No single `.shape`; use `dim()` for the full dimensions |
:::

## Task 1

Import the `Produc` dataset (from the package `plm`) using the following code:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
data(Produc, package = "plm")
```

## Task 2

Convert the data from long to wide

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Tip: pipes and tidyverse

The `|>` pipe passes the left-hand result as the **first argument** of the next function — equivalent to writing nested calls, but readable left-to-right. If you know pandas method chaining (`.groupby().agg()`), the mental model is the same.

`tidyr` and `dplyr` together are R's closest equivalent to pandas: 

- `pivot_wider()` ~ `df.pivot()`
- `select()` ~ `df[["col"]]`
- `filter()` ~ `df[df.x > 0]`
- `mutate()` ~ `df["new"] = ...`.
:::

```{r}
#| output: false
library(plm)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(tibble)
data("Produc", package = "plm")

Produc_wide <- Produc |>
  select(year, state, unemp) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = state, values_from = unemp) |>
  column_to_rownames("year")
```

## Task 3

Convert the wide dataframe to a matrix

```{r}
Produc_matrix <- as.matrix(Produc_wide)
```

## Task 4

Calculate mean unemployment first using the wide dataframe, then the matrix. Compare the speed.

```{r}
library(bench)
bm <- bench::mark(
    matrix = mean(Produc_matrix, na.rm = TRUE),
    dataframe = mean(Produc_wide |> unlist(), na.rm = TRUE),
    filter_gc = FALSE
)

bm$total_time[2] / bm$total_time[1]
```

## Task 5

The following command returns the path to a GeoTIFF file on your hard drive:

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Tip: terra vs rasterio / numpy

`terra` is R's primary raster package. If you have used `rasterio` or `numpy` arrays for raster data in Python, here is a rough mapping:

| Python | R (terra) |
|---|---|
| `rasterio.open("f.tif")` | `rast("f.tif")` |
| `src.read()` → numpy array | `values(r)` → matrix |
| `src.meta` | print the `SpatRaster` object |
| `src.crs` | `crs(r)` |
| `src.transform` / `src.res` | `res(r)`, `ext(r)` |

Unlike a raw numpy array, a `SpatRaster` keeps its spatial metadata (CRS, extent, resolution) attached at all times.
:::

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
system.file("ex/elev.tif", package = "terra")
```

Use this path to import the file using `rast()`, store it as `r`.

```{r}
library(terra)
r <- system.file("ex/elev.tif", package = "terra") |>
  rast()
```

## Task 6

Explore this object:

- Determine the minimum and maximum elevation values
- Make a static map using base `plot()` and `tmap`
- Make an interactive map using tmap (`tmap_mode("view")`)
- Using tmap, explore different [styles](https://r-tmap.github.io/tmap/reference/tm_raster.html#arg-style) and [palettes](https://r-tmap.github.io/tmap/reference/tm_raster.html#arg-palette)

```{r}
r  # printing the object shows min/max in the metadata

library(tmap)

tm_shape(r) +
  tm_raster()
```

## Task 7

Import the Landsat 7 image:

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
system.file("tif/L7_ETMs.tif", package = "stars")
```

Store it as `l7`. Then rename its layers to `c("B", "G", "R", "NIR", "SWIR", "MIR")` (see [here](https://r-spatial.github.io/stars/reference/L7_ETMs.html)).

```{r}
l7 <- system.file("tif/L7_ETMs.tif", package = "stars") |>
  rast()

names(l7) <- c("B", "G", "R", "NIR", "SWIR", "MIR")
```

## Task 8

Compare `r` and `l7`:

- How many layers does each have?
- What is the resolution of each?
- What is the extent of each?
- Plot all layers of `l7` individually

```{r}
nlyr(r)
nlyr(l7)

res(r)
res(l7)

ext(r)
ext(l7)

plot(l7)
```

## Task 9

Select the Red, Green and Blue bands from `l7` to create a true color composite using `plotRGB()` and `tm_rgb()`.

```{r}
library(tmap)

plotRGB(l7[[c("R", "G", "B")]], stretch = "histogram")

tm_shape(l7[[c("R", "G", "B")]]) + tm_rgb()
```

## Task 10

Select the NIR, Green and Blue bands from `l7` to create a false color composite.

```{r}
tm_shape(l7[[c("NIR", "G", "B")]]) + tm_rgb()
```

## Task 11

Query the full metadata of `r` and `l7`:

- Number of rows, columns, and layers
- Spatial extent
- Pixel resolution
- CRS (use `crs(..., describe = TRUE)` for a readable summary)

```{r}
#| output: false
# r
nrow(r); ncol(r); nlyr(r)
ext(r)
res(r)
crs(r, describe = TRUE)

# l7
nrow(l7); ncol(l7); nlyr(l7)
ext(l7)
res(l7)
crs(l7, describe = TRUE)
```

## Task 12

Check whether `r` uses a geographic or projected CRS. Reproject it to EPSG:2169 (Luxembourg national projection) and compare `res()` before and after.

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Tip: CRS and reprojection

In Python you would use `pyproj.CRS` or `geopandas`/`rasterio`'s `.to_crs()`. In `terra`, `project(r, "EPSG:2169")` handles both the coordinate transform and the pixel resampling in one step. A geographic CRS (degrees) will show `res()` values around `0.008`, while a projected CRS (metres) will show values in the hundreds — same pixel, different units.
:::

```{r}
#| output: false
crs(r, describe = TRUE)   # geographic: WGS84, units = degrees

r_projected <- project(r, "EPSG:2169")

res(r)            # degrees
res(r_projected)  # meters
```

## Task 13

Create a masked version of `r` where all elevations **below 300 m** are set to `NA`. Visualize both the original and the masked raster side by side.

```{r}
library(tmap)

r_masked <- ifel(r < 300, NA, r)

tmap_arrange(
  tm_shape(r)        + tm_raster(style = "cont", palette = "viridis", legend.show = FALSE),
  tm_shape(r_masked) + tm_raster(style = "cont", palette = "viridis", legend.show = FALSE)
)
```

## Task 14

Write the reprojected raster from Task 12 to disk as a GeoTIFF. Then read it back and verify that the CRS and resolution are preserved.

```{r}
#| output: false
#| 
writeRaster(r_projected, "data-out/elev_2169.tif", overwrite = TRUE)

r_check <- rast("data-out/elev_2169.tif")

crs(r_check, describe = TRUE)
res(r_check)
```
